feedback: If a learner plots or records the spring's total length, prompt: extension = current length − natural length; the natural length must be measured and subtracted first.
If force is recorded in grams or kilograms, remind that those are masses; weight (a force) in newtons is W = m × g, or read force directly from the newton meter.
If only one reading is taken per load, prompt a repeat and a mean at each step so anomalies can be judged — this is a scaffold, not a reteach of the whole method.
If more than one variable changes, point back to the IV/DV/CV plan: keep the same spring and change only the force.
activities.intendedInsight: Force is measured in newtons; extension (not total length) is the quantity that responds to force; controlling variables and repeating readings is what makes the relationship trustworthy.
learnerActions: Clamp a spring, measure and record its natural (unstretched) length first.
State the variables before starting: independent = force applied (added in equal steps), dependent = extension, control = the same spring throughout.
Add weight one equal step at a time (hang slotted masses and convert to weight using W = m × g, or read force directly in newtons from a newton meter), letting the spring settle each time.
Measure the new length at each load and read the ruler squarely — line your eye level with the mark, or use a set square against the ruler to avoid parallax error.
Calculate extension at each step: extension = current length − natural length.
Repeat each reading (and read again on unloading) and take a mean, so scatter and anomalies become visible.
Record force in newtons and extension in a results table.
activities.title: Hooke's Law practical with real apparatus

feedback: If a learner connects the points to make a kinked line, explain that real readings scatter: draw ONE best-fit straight line with points either side so anomalies stand out.
If the line does not pass through the origin and the learner doesn't notice, check whether total length was plotted instead of extension.

If a learner extrapolates the straight line indefinitely or forces a straight line through the curved high-load points, prompt them to load past the limit so they can SEE the curve and mark where proportionality ends.
Encourage the phrasing 'the same extension is added per newton' rather than 'the length doubles per newton'.
activities.intendedInsight: A best-fit line averages real measurement scatter rather than connecting individual points; the force–extension relationship is proportional only up to a limit of proportionality, after which it bends (and, at still greater loads beyond the elastic limit, the spring may deform permanently).
learnerActions: Plot Force (newtons) on the y-axis against Extension on the x-axis using your recorded data.
Draw a single straight line of best fit through the scattered points — do NOT join the dots point-to-point; aim for a line with roughly equal numbers of points on each side.

Describe the pattern in words: up to the limit of proportionality, equal steps of force add the SAME extension each time (not 'the length doubles'), and with zero extension at zero force this means extension is directly proportional to force — a straight line through the origin.
Continue adding load in a second investigation (or extend the dataset) until the once-straight line starts to bend, and mark that point where proportionality ends — the limit of proportionality.

Separately, note that if the spring is loaded past its elastic limit (which for many springs is at or only a little beyond the limit of proportionality) it may be permanently stretched and no longer return to its natural length; this is a distinct idea from the limit of proportionality.
Explain why the line is drawn to average scatter rather than connecting every point.
activities.title: Plotting force vs extension and drawing a line of best fit

feedback: If a learner expects perfect agreement, first check that m includes every mass being accelerated (trolley plus any hanging masses); then remind them that friction opposes the applied force, so the resultant (net) force is smaller than F and the observed acceleration is a little below the F/m prediction; measurement uncertainty adds further to the difference.

If a learner describes the force as setting the trolley's speed or current direction, remind them that the resultant force determines acceleration (change in motion), so the stated starting condition (e.g. from rest) matters when predicting how the motion changes.
activities.intendedInsight: A measured applied force on a known total moving mass (trolley plus any hanging masses) predicts an acceleration via a = F/m when friction is small; more precisely, it is the resultant force (applied force minus friction) that determines acceleration — a change in motion, not an instant speed or direction. Because real friction makes the resultant smaller than the applied force, the observed acceleration is usually a little below F/m, and comparing prediction with real motion tests Newton's Second Law.
learnerActions: Apply a measured force to a trolley of known mass (include a risk assessment for any hanging masses).
State the trolley's starting condition (e.g. starting from rest) before describing how its motion changes.

Calculate the predicted acceleration using a = F / m, where F is the applied (driving) force and m is the total mass being accelerated (the trolley plus any hanging masses that move with it), assuming friction is small.
Measure the trolley's actual acceleration (e.g. with light gates or a motion sensor/data logger) and compare it with the calculated acceleration.
Discuss sources of difference (e.g. friction opposing the applied force, measurement error) between prediction and observation.
activities.title: Testing Newton's Second Law with a trolley

feedback: If a learner chooses the dot-to-dot line, re-explain that the best-fit line averages scatter.
If a learner mislabels the variables, point back to: force is changed (IV), extension responds (DV), the spring is kept the same (CV).
activities.intendedInsight: Secure procedural reasoning — correct sequencing, variable identification, best-fit choice, and recognising the limit of proportionality — underpins a trustworthy investigation.
learnerActions: Put the method steps in the correct order: plan the variables, measure natural length, add load in equal steps, measure new length, calculate extension, repeat readings, plot, draw best-fit line, identify the limit of proportionality.
Identify which quantity is the independent variable, dependent variable, and control variable for the spring investigation.
Given a graph with scattered points, select or sketch the correct line of best fit (not the dot-to-dot line).
Given a force–extension graph that curves, mark the limit of proportionality.
activities.title: Plan and reason about the method (companion check)
